claim: Temporal synchrony of signals arriving from different neurons or brain regions is essential for proper neural processing.
source: Temporal synchrony of signals arriving from different neurons or brain regions is essential for proper neural processing.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from general scientific knowledge.

claim: It is not well understood how synchrony is achieved and maintained in a complex network of time-delayed neural interactions.
source: Nevertheless, it is not well understood how such synchrony is achieved and maintained in a complex network of time-delayed neural interactions.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Myelin plasticity has been suggested as an efficient mechanism for controlling timing in brain communications through adaptive changes of axonal conduction velocity.
source: Myelin plasticity, accomplished by oligodendrocytes (OLs), has been suggested as an efficient mechanism for controlling timing in brain communications through adaptive changes of axonal conduction velocity and consequently conduction time delays, or latencies
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work in the field, as indicated by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Local rules and feedback mechanisms that oligodendrocytes use to achieve synchronization are not known.
source: however, local rules and feedback mechanisms that OLs use to achieve synchronization are not known.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the current work aims to address.

claim: The OMP model achieves synchronization without using arrival times at the synapse or modulatory signaling from astrocytes.
source: This is achieved without using arrival times at the synapse or modulatory signaling from astrocytes; instead, it relies on the presence of global and transient OL responses to local action potentials in the axons they myelinate.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the proposed model.

claim: When the characteristic time of OL's transient intracellular responses to neural spikes is between 10 and 40 ms and firing rates are relatively low (10 Hz), the OMP model efficiently synchronizes correlated and time-locked signals.
source: Our results indicate that when the characteristic time of OL's transient intracellular responses to neural spikes is between 10 and 40 ms and the firing rates in individual axons are relatively low (10 Hz), the OMP model efficiently synchronizes correlated and time-locked signals while latencies in axons carrying independent signals are unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling and simulation work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Latencies in axons carrying independent signals are unaffected by the OMP model.
source: the OMP model efficiently synchronizes correlated and time-locked signals while latencies in axons carrying independent signals are unaffected.
evidence: This is a key result from the simulations showing selective synchronization.

claim: Oligodendrocytes play an active role in modulating the conduction delays of correlated spike trains.
source: This suggests a novel form of selective synchronization in the CNS in which oligodendrocytes play an active role by modulating the conduction delays of correlated spike trains as they traverse to their targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Temporal precision required in neural processing can range from sub-millisecond in sound localization and echolocation tasks to milliseconds and hundreds of milliseconds in perceptual and motor system signal processing.
source: Temporal precision required in neural processing can range from sub-millisecond in sound localization and echolocation tasks to milliseconds and hundreds of milliseconds in perceptual and motor system signal processing.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neural processing requirements.

claim: Signals traveling from distant regions commonly traverse complex conduction paths along which conduction velocity is not constant and undergoes dynamical changes and perturbations, particularly during development.
source: Signals traveling from distant regions commonly traverse complex conduction paths along which conduction velocity (CV) is not constant and undergoes dynamical changes and perturbations, particularly during the development.
evidence: This describes known properties of neural signal conduction.

claim: Adaptive adjustment of conduction velocity through myelin plasticity has been argued as a solution to temporal precision problems for more than a decade.
source: It has been argued for more than a decade that a solution to this problem is the adaptive adjustment of the CV through a mechanism of myelin plasticity (MP) Fields, 2005; Fields, 2008, which postulates that myelination is an adaptive and neural activity-dependent process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fields 2005 and 2008.

claim: Modifying myelin sheath thickness and node of Ranvier structure provides the most efficient means to alter conduction delays through changes in conduction velocity.
source: Modifying myelin sheath thickness and node of Ranvier structure provides the most efficient means to alter conduction delays through changes in CV.
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in neuroscience.

claim: There is growing evidence that myelin plasticity is important for fear conditioning.
source: There is growing evidence that myelin plasticity is important for fear conditioning Pan et al., 2020; Steadman et al., 2020
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2020 and Steadman et al., 2020.

claim: Myelin plasticity is important for spatial learning.
source: spatial learning Wang et al., 2020; Steadman et al., 2020
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2020 and Steadman et al., 2020.

claim: Myelin plasticity is essential for motor skill learning.
source: and is shown to be essential for motor skill learning Bacmeister et al., 2020; Kato et al., 2020; McKenzie et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2016.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Very little progress has been made in understanding the local learning rules in myelin plasticity and what feedback oligodendrocytes use to properly adjust myelination in the CNS.
source: Yet, very little progress has been made in understanding the local learning rules in this new form of plasticity and what feedback oligodendrocytes (OLs) use to properly adjust myelination in the CNS.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current understanding that motivates the present work.

claim: Oligodendrocytes are mostly located far from the target neurons and lack direct feedback on what the desired conduction velocity is.
source: OLs are mostly located far from the target neurons and lack direct feedback on what the desired CV is because the information about the arrival times of the action potentials, that is spikes, is not available at these intermediate locations.
evidence: This is based on known anatomical facts about oligodendrocyte location.

claim: In most studies of activity-dependent myelination, the precise timing of individual spikes is ignored.
source: Moreover, in most studies of activity-dependent myelination (ADM) Pajevic et al., 2014; Fields, 2015; Dutta et al., 2019; Stevens et al., 2002; Talidou et al., 2021 the precise timing of individual spikes is ignored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies in the field.

claim: The introduction of time delays can change both stability and synchronizability at a system level.
source: It is well known that the introduction of time delays can change both stability and synchronizability at a system level, which then provides an indirect mechanism for MP to affect both the stability Pajevic et al., 2014 and synchronization, for example in a network of spiking neurons Talidou et al., 2021.
evidence: This is stated as well-known and supported by citations.

claim: Oligodendrocyte morphology differs drastically from that of Schwann cells.
source: Our OMP model was inspired by the fact that OL morphology differs drastically from that of Schwann cell (SC), which myelinate axons in the PNS.
evidence: This is an established anatomical fact.

claim: Oligodendrocytes extend many processes to myelinate multiple axons, while Schwann cells myelinate only a single axon.
source: The most important morphological difference between these two myelinating cell types is that the OL extends many of its processes to myelinate multiple axons, while the SC myelinates only a single axon (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by both text description and Figure 1A and B showing the morphological differences.

claim: The morphological difference between oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells comes from the distinct functional roles myelination plays in the PNS and CNS.
source: We hypothesize that this difference comes from the distinct functional roles myelination plays in the PNS and CNS.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis.

claim: In the PNS, the goal of myelination is to maximize conduction velocity.
source: In the PNS, the goal is to maximize the CV
evidence: This is stated as an established understanding of PNS myelination function.

claim: In the CNS, the presumed goal of myelination is to optimize the synchrony of signals arriving from multiple sources.
source: while in the CNS the presumed goal is to optimize the synchrony of signals arriving from multiple sources.
evidence: This is presented as a presumption that motivates the model.

claim: Oligodendrocytes tend to maximize the number of axons they myelinate, making it unlikely that a given oligodendrocyte would myelinate the same axon twice.
source: but with a tendency to maximize the number of axons it can myelinate, making it unlikely that a given OL would myelinate the same axon twice Dumas et al., 2015; Walsh et al., 2016.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dumas et al., 2015 and Walsh et al., 2016.

claim: Oligodendrocyte morphology enables a single oligodendrocyte to integrate and compare signals from different axons.
source: We postulate that this morphology enables a single OL to integrate and compare signals from different axons and act as a mediator in providing the needed feedback for adjusting the relative timing of different signals via dynamic regulation of the CV along these axons.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a postulate of the model.

claim: For Poisson spiking with fixed time delays, the differential expression of the myelination factor will always myelinate the lagging axons more than the preceding ones.
source: The Equation 4 is an important result that indicates that with Poisson spiking and fixed time delays along different axons, the differential expression of the myelination factor will always myelinate the lagging axons more than the preceding ones.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model (Equation 4).

claim: For correlated spikes, a single exponential approach to synchrony was most commonly observed.
source: For correlated spikes, a single exponential approach to synchrony was most commonly observed (E1).
evidence: This is a result from model fitting to the simulation data.

claim: The instability in the OMP model rapidly disappeared for any level of jitter when longer oligo-chains are used.
source: This instability, however, rapidly disappeared for any level of jitter when longer OCs are used (Figure 3B, solid lines; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in multiple figures.

claim: Synchronization became progressively harder with increase in firing rate and number of axons to synchronize.
source: whereas synchronization became progressively harder with increase in firing rate and number of axons to synchronize.
evidence: This is observed from the simulation results.

claim: The OMP model selectively synchronizes groups of axons carrying correlated spikes while leaving those carrying independent or uncorrelated spikes unaffected.
source: The adaptive changes to axonal delays are selectively applied to groups of axons that carry correlated spikes so that they arrive at their targets simultaneously, while those carrying independent or uncorrelated spikes are not affected (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Neighboring axons share similar temporal firing and functional properties in known circuit anatomy.
source: This selectivity conforms to known relationship between circuit anatomy and function, in which neighboring axons share similar temporal firing and functional properties; for example, the tonotopic organization of auditory cortex and the cortical homunculus in somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neural organization.

claim: Correlated firing drives refinement of connections between the retina and LGN during development.
source: Such correlated firing also drives refinement of connections between the retina and LGN during development Meister et al., 1991.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meister et al., 1991.

claim: Myelination usually begins after axons reach their target and become functional, starting from the cell body and proceeding toward the axon terminal.
source: Myelination usually begins after axons reach their target and become functional, starting from the cell body and proceeding toward the axon terminal.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about myelination development.

claim: In the optic nerve, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells migrate out of the brain during development, yet axonal myelination proceeds in the reverse direction from the retina toward the optic chiasm.
source: This is clearly evident in the optic nerve, where OL progenitor cells migrate out of the brain and into the optic nerve during development, yet axonal myelination proceeds in the reverse direction, beginning at the retina on retinal ganglion cells and proceeding toward the optic chiasm Ishibashi et al., 2009.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishibashi et al., 2009.

claim: The proximal-to-distal gradient of myelination agrees well with the OMP model as oligodendrocytes at the source end of the oligo-chain will experience less synchronized signals.
source: Such a proximal-to-distal gradient agrees well with our OMP model as the OLs at the source end of the OC will experience less synchronized signals.
evidence: This is an inference connecting known biological facts to model predictions.

claim: The OMP model predicts that structural deformation or lesion to a portion of axons carrying correlated activity would lead to re-myelination downstream or immediately after the site of the lesion, while myelin upstream will not be affected.
source: Another testable prediction of this model would be that structural deformation or lesion to a portion of axons carrying correlated activity would lead to re-myelination downstream or immediately after the site of the lesion, while myelin upstream will not be affected.
evidence: This is presented as a testable prediction from the model.

claim: The efficiency of synchronization is slightly reduced when a fraction of axons carry uncorrelated signals.
source: Results in Figure 4 suggest that the efficiency of synchronization is slightly reduced when a fraction of axons carry uncorrelated signals.
evidence: This is observed from simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Oligodendrocytes might remove their processes from axons carrying uncorrelated signals while keeping or growing new processes only on axons that carry synchronized signals.
source: Hence, we postulate that in the brain, OLs might be removing their processes from such axons while keeping or growing new processes only on those axons that carry synchronized signals.
evidence: This is presented as a postulate based on the model results.

claim: OMP predicts that synchronization is most effective at lower firing rates.
source: OMP predicts that synchronization is most effective at lower firing rates, and thus we expect it to occur when the brain operates in low spiking rate regimes.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model results.

claim: Oligodendrocytes can undergo sudden depolarization which leads to significant changes in conduction velocity.
source: It was observed that OLs can undergo sudden depolarization which leads to significant changes (10%) in Yamazaki et al., 2007
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamazaki et al., 2007.

claim: The OMP-1 model shows that passive responses of oligodendrocyte cells are sufficient for synchronizing neural signals.
source: While this can be incorporated into a general OMP scheme (Figure 1D), the OMP-1 shows that passive responses of OL cells are sufficient for synchronizing neural signals, as well that astrocytes, commonly considered the actors in providing the feedback in MP, are not needed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: Astrocytes are not needed for the synchronization mechanism in the OMP model.
source: as well that astrocytes, commonly considered the actors in providing the feedback in MP, are not needed.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: Poisson spiking is more reliable for myelin plasticity than regular spiking, even though it is slower and less efficient in many situations.
source: Hence, Poisson spiking, even though slower and in many situations less efficient than regular spiking, is more reliable for the MP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model behavior.

claim: The noisy brain is a healthy brain, and too much regularity/synchronization in brain dynamics can lead to its failure.
source: Our model of synchronization provides further support for the narrative that the noisy brain is a healthy brain, and too much regularity/synchronization in the brain dynamics can lead to its failure.
evidence: This is a broader interpretation of the model results in the context of brain function.

claim: Confocal imaging shows that action potentials in axons cause local calcium transients in oligodendrocytes via vesicular release of glutamate acting on NMDA and glutamate receptors.
source: Confocal imaging of local calcium responses in myelinating oligodendrocytes in cell culture, together with the imaging of local translation of myelin basic protein, show that action potentials in axons cause local calcium transients in OL via vesicular release of glutamate from axons acting on NMDA and glutamate receptors (mGluR) on the oligodendrocyte processes Wake et al., 2011.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wake et al., 2011.

claim: Local calcium transients promote the formation of an axo-glial signaling complex, triggering local translation of myelin basic protein to initiate myelination.
source: This promotes the formation of an axo-glial signaling complex, triggering the local translation of myelin basic protein to initiate myelination Wake et al., 2011, preferentially on the electrically active axon Wake et al., 2015.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wake et al., 2011 and Wake et al., 2015.

claim: Local signaling can trigger myelin synthesis rapidly, within minutes.
source: This local signaling can trigger myelin synthesis rapidly, within minutes Wake et al., 2011.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wake et al., 2011.

claim: In vivo imaging in zebrafish indicates that myelin sheath elongation during development is regulated by the kinetics of calcium transients in oligodendrocytes evoked by neuronal activity.
source: Similar responses are observed using in vivo imaging in zebrafish Hines et al., 2015; Mensch et al., 2015; Krasnow et al., 2018 which further indicate that myelin sheath elongation during development is regulated by the kinetics of calcium transients in oligodendrocytes that are evoked by neuronal activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hines et al., 2015; Mensch et al., 2015; Krasnow et al., 2018.

claim: Local calcium transients in oligodendrocyte cell processes are independent from one another and can be integrated within the cell to trigger global calcium responses in the cell body via temporal summation.
source: In Krasnow et al., 2018 they show that local calcium transients in oligodendrocyte cell processes are independent from one another and that the local calcium signals can be integrated within the cell to trigger global calcium responses in the cell body via temporal summation (Supp Figure 1 in Krasnow et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krasnow et al., 2018.

claim: Myelin sheath elongation is promoted by high-frequency calcium transients, and sheath shortening is associated with low-frequency calcium transients.
source: The same study shows that myelin sheath elongation is promoted by high-frequency calcium transients, and sheath shortening is associated with low-frequency calcium transients.
evidence: This refers to findings from Krasnow et al., 2018.

claim: Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells often couple synaptically to axons via both excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic connections.
source: It is also important to note that oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) often couple synaptically to axons via both, the excitatory, glutamatergic Kukley et al., 2007; Ziskin et al., 2007 and inhibitory, GABAergic connections Maldonado and Angulo, 2015.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kukley et al., 2007; Ziskin et al., 2007; Maldonado and Angulo, 2015.

claim: Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells can respond to different patterns of action potentials with different functional effects on cell differentiation and proliferation.
source: This enables the cells to respond to different patterns of action potentials with different functional effects on cell differentiation and proliferation Nagy et al., 2017
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nagy et al., 2017.

claim: ATP and adenosine are activity-dependent signaling molecules released from axons firing action potentials that activate purinergic receptors, leading to global increases in cell calcium and activation of myelination promoting genes.
source: There are other activity-dependent signaling molecules released from axons firing action potentials, notably ATP and adenosine, that activate purinergic receptors, leading to global increases in cell calcium and activation of the myelination promoting genes Stevens et al., 2002; Ishibashi et al., 2006; Fields and Ni, 2010.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stevens et al., 2002; Ishibashi et al., 2006; Fields and Ni, 2010.
